25-1391 BMG RIGHTS MANAGEMENT, ET AL. V. VETTER, CYRIL E., ET AL.

the qualified Justices are of the opinion that the case cannot 
be heard and determined at the next Term of the Court, the

1  Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. 
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES 
RYAN O’DONNELL, ET AL. v. CITY OF CHICAGO, 
ILLINOIS, ET AL. 
ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED 
STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT 
No. 25–1098. Decided October 19, 2026 
The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. 
Statement of J USTICE SOTOMAYOR, with whom J USTICE 
GORSUCH joins, respecting the denial of certiorari. 
In Chicago, a driver who fails to pay as few as two park-
ing tickets risks forfeiting his vehicle to the city.  The city
then can do as it pleases with the vehicle, with no obligation 
to pay compensation, offset the unpaid ticket debt, or return
any surplus to the owner if the vehicle is sold for a profit.
See Chicago, Ill., Municipal Code §§9–100–120(b), (f ) 
(2026). The Seventh Circuit upheld that scheme as con-
sistent with the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, rea-
soning that it is “an exercise of the City’s police power to
enforce its traffic code.” 163 F. 4th 411, 414 (2025).  I have 
serious concerns about that conclusion, which implicates a
Circuit split over whether, and under what circumstances,
exercises of the State’s police power are immune to takings 
claims. Because that split would continue to benefit from 
further percolation, however, and because this case is not 
the best vehicle to resolve the split, I concur in the Court’s
denial of certiorari. 
Chicago’s vehicle-forfeiture scheme is vast and lucrative,
helping the city generate, according to one estimate, $264
million in traffic-ticket revenue (or 7 percent of the city’s 
operating budget) in 2016.  See M. Sanchez & S. Kambham-
pati, How Chicago Ticket Debt Sends Black Motorists Into
Bankruptcy, ProPublica (Feb. 27, 2018), https://fea-
tures.propublica.org/driven-into-debt/chicago-ticket-debt-

2 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO 
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. 
bankruptcy/ (archived at https://
perma.cc/K8MU-KVTW).  Petitioners Ryan O’Donnell and
Michael Goree are two of the many Chicago motorists sub -
ject to that scheme.  According to the complaint filed in this
case, O’Donnell received two tickets for an expired meter
and one ticket for time-restricted parking, totaling approx-
imately $524. Goree did not have any tickets himself; ra-
ther, a co-signer on his vehicle had approximately $560 of 
outstanding ticket debt from a different vehicle.  After those 
tickets went unpaid, the city towed and impounded peti -
tioners’ vehicles, adding additional boot, tow, and storage 
fees. It then sold O’Donnell’s vehicle for its scrap value of 
$273 and relinquished Goree’s vehicle to the lienholder.
Neither petitioner received any compensation for the loss of 
their cars. 
Petitioners sued the city, alleging that its scheme facially 
violates the Takings Clause, which bars taking “private
property” for “public use, without just compensation.”  They
asserted that §9–100–120 empowers the city to take vehi-
cles “without providing any compensation to the owner or
even a hearing to determine fair compensation.”  Complaint
in No. 1:23–cv–01192 (ND Ill.), ECF Doc. 1, ¶73.  The Dis-
trict Court dismissed the suit, see App. to Pet. for Cert. 16–
18; and the Seventh Circuit affirmed, see 163 F. 4th, at 
414–415. As relevant here, the Seventh Circuit rejected pe-
titioners’ argument that Ch icago’s vehicle-forfeiture 
scheme is like the tax-forfeiture statute this Court invali-
dated in Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U. S. 631 (2023), for 
failure to return any surplus to the homeowner after a tax
sale. The better analogy, the Seventh Circuit reasoned, was 
to Bennis v. Michigan, 516 U. S. 442 (1996), where this 
Court held that the government may seize property used in
the violation of the law without providing any compensa-
tion to the owner. See 163 F. 4th, at 414–415 (citing Bennis, 
516 U. S., at 453); see also id., at 452 (forfeitures that

3  Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. 
comport with due process do not trigger the duty of just
compensation).
Unlike the laws discussed in Bennis, however, Chicago
does not impound only those vehicles involved in violations
of its municipal traffic code.  Rather, the city may impound 
any vehicle of a delinquent resident so long as ticket debts 
remain unpaid, regardless of whether the vehicle was in-
volved in an infraction. §9–100–120(b).  Indeed, that is pre-
cisely what happened to Goree, who lost his car because a
co-owner incurred ticket debt on a different vehicle. After 
the vehicle is impounded, moreover, forfeiture is a conse-
quence only of the failure to pay, not the antecedent legal
infraction. §9–100–120(f ).  Those features strongly suggest 
that “the purpose of vehi cle impoundments” under Chi-
cago’s scheme “is to collect a debt, not enforce public safety
laws.” Pet. for Cert. 10. If so, then Tyler would seem to 
control, and the city’s failure to compensate owners for the 
loss of their vehicles would likely violate the Takings 
Clause.  The city’s practice of surrendering cars to lienhold-
ers or selling them for their scrap value, rather than at a
fair auction, only amplifies the potential constitutional in-
firmity. Cf. Pung v. Isabella County, 609 U. S. 30, 33 (2026) 
(just compensation is measured based on “fairly conducted”
tax sale).
Because of its mistaken reliance on Bennis, the Seventh 
Circuit considered Chicago’s ve hicle-forfeiture scheme “a
‘classic example’ ” of the State’s “police power.”  163 F. 4th, 
at 414 (quoting Hadley v. South Bend, 154 F. 4th 549, 556 
(CA7 2025)). As I have previous ly written, the lower courts 
are divided over “the extent to which the Takings Clause
applies to exercises of the police power.” Baker v. City of 
McKinney, 604 U. S. 1035, 1038 (2024) (statement of 
SOTOMAYOR, J., respecting denial of certiorari).  Here, the 
Seventh Circuit embraced the expansive notion that “exer-
cise[s] of the City’s police po wer to enforce its traffic code” 
are immune to takings claims. 163 F. 4th, at 414.  Some

4 O’DONNELL v. CITY OF CHICAGO 
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. 
courts have likewise appeared to adopt a categorical rule 
that the Takings Clause does not apply when the govern-
ment acts under any of its police powers. See, e.g., Amer-
iSource Corp. v. United States, 525 F. 3d 1149, 1153 (CA 
Fed. 2008); Lech v. Jackson, 791 Fed. Appx. 711, 717 (CA10 
2019). Others have held, more narrowly, that the just-com-
pensation requirement is subject to a public-safety or ne -
cessity exception, see, e.g., Baker v. McKinney , 84 F. 4th 
378, 388 (CA5 2023); Pena v. Los Angeles, 158 F. 4th 1033, 
1035 (CA9 2025), or that no property is taken when it is
damaged incident to a lawful search or arrest, see, e .g., 
Slaybaugh v. Rutherford County, 114 F. 4th 593, 598 (CA6 
2024); Hadley, 154 F. 4th, at 554; Pena, 158 F. 4th, at 1050 
(Friedland, J., concurring in judgment). It is still an “open 
question” whether these or any other approaches are con -
sistent with this Court’s precedents.  Baker, 604 U. S., at 
1038. Few of these decisions likewise explain the source of 
any such police-power exception to the Takings Clause—
whether the common law, the Constitution, or elsewhere. 
Such questions thus continue to “benefit from further per-
colation” in the lower courts before this Court chooses to in-
tervene. Id., at 1039. Petitioners, moreover, have lodged a
facial challenge to Chicago’s ordinance, which might re-
quire this Court to invalidate even those features of the law
that have nothing to do with vehicle forfeiture. See, e.g., 
§9–100–120(a) (providing for immobilization of vehicles).  I 
therefore concur in the Court’s denial of certiorari.  I none-
theless write to emphasize that courts should carefully and
narrowly define the circumstances in which the State’s ex -
ercise of its police powers are held exempt from the just-
compensation requirement, as well as explain the source of
any such exemption. Where, as here, a person alleges a 
“classic taking in which the government directly appropri -
ates private property for its own use” or to pay an outstand-
ing debt, like a tax lien, Tyler, 598 U. S., at 639 (internal
quotation marks omitted), the talismanic invocation of the

5  Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J. 
State’s “law enforcement authority,” 163 F. 4th, at 414, may 
be insufficient to avoid the requirement of just compensa-
tion. I again encourage courts considering this issue to take
care that due deference to state police powers does not 
eclipse constitutional rights.
